name: Removing Names Before Data Goes In
title: Removing Names Before Data Goes In
answer: Removing names before data goes into an AI tool means taking out the details that identify a student, including names, student ID numbers, birth dates, addresses and school names, and often more than that. It is described as the simplest and most effective privacy habit with AI, because it lets a teacher get useful help while nothing in the result points to a real child. It works as a second layer of protection alongside an approved tool and a signed agreement, not as a replacement for either.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: This idea is a habit of stripping identifying details from student information before that information is entered into an AI tool. The details to remove start with names, student ID numbers, birth dates, addresses and school names, but the list does not stop there. A rare disability, a small grade level, or a specific family situation can point to a particular child even when no name is present, so the teacher has to think about what else might give a student away. The problem it solves is the most common privacy mistake made with AI, which is letting identifying information flow into a tool in the first place. When the removal becomes automatic across a staff, that mistake largely disappears.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The book offers a worked example rather than a grade by grade breakdown. A special education teacher wants help drafting a goal for a student's individualized education program. One version of the request contains everything the teacher knows about the student, and the other contains only what the tool needs in order to draft the goal. The draft that comes back from the reduced version is just as useful, and nothing in it points to a real child. The same move applies whenever a teacher uses AI to think through a problem, and the book treats it as a habit worth building across the whole staff rather than a one off step.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no evidence label, no study and no figure beyond a worked example, so this idea rests on practice rather than research. The only illustration offered is Figure 3.6, which shows the special education teacher's two versions of a request side by side, one carrying everything the teacher knows and one carrying only what the tool needs. The claim made from that example is that the draft returned is just as useful and that nothing in it points to a real child. No measurement, comparison group or published finding is presented to support the habit.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: Removing names is not a substitute for an approved tool or a signed agreement, and the book is explicit that it does not replace either. It is a second layer of protection for the moments when a teacher uses AI to think through a problem, which means the underlying approvals still have to be in place. The judgment about which details actually identify a child stays with the person doing the work, because indirect clues such as a rare disability, a small grade level or a specific family situation can single out a student even after the obvious identifiers are gone. That judgment cannot be handed to the tool, and the teacher remains the one who decides what the tool truly needs to see.
